_note: The Hinge — my coding of 45 keeper entries on the 14 nuclear close calls that three or four keepers list (event matching: the Field's study 7). One reader, me, 2026-10-10, under the rule in PREDICTIONS.md, committed before any entry was read. Steps are my own summary of each event from the entries, not a source. Every quotation is checked word for word against the fetched source by build.py. Deviation from the fixed scheme, recorded at coding time: the consequent scheme had three values (war, detonation, unstated); four entries state a consequent that is an attack read where there was none and passed on ('misreading'), two state a consequent that is neither ('other'). P4 is decided on war against every stated consequent, so the added values cannot change its verdict.

PH.quote: If the people involved had exercised less caution, or if some unfortunate coincidental event had occurred, escalation to nuclear war can easily be imagined.
PH.note: Phillips writes one hinge for all twenty items, at the door of the list: people, or coincidence.

WP.quote: A nuclear close call is an incident that might have led to at least one nuclear explosion, but did not.
WP.note: Wikipedia's definition names a consequent (one explosion), not a hinge.

events.name: Suez: four coincident reports
steps: Four reports reach NORAD
Read together as a Soviet offensive
Fear: the NATO nuclear strike plan is triggered
Each report explained: swans, an escort, a mechanical fault, an exercise

entries.cons_quote: these events might trigger the NATO operations plan for nuclear strikes against the U.S.S.R.
the U.S. worried a NATO nuclear strike against Russia could soon follow

entries.label: s3
entries.cons_quote: U.S. forces believed these events could trigger a NATO nuclear strike against the Soviet Union

events.name: BMEWS: all lines dead through one relay
steps: All lines from SAC HQ to NORAD and the warning sites go dead
SAC alerts its bases; crews start engines
A B-52 near Thule reaches the site by radio: no attack
Cause: one overheated motor in one relay station

events.name: Duluth: a bear and a miswired klaxon
steps: A guard shoots at a figure on the fence; sabotage alarm
Volk Field is miswired: the klaxon orders nuclear interceptors up
A call to Duluth reveals the error
A car on the runway stops the aircraft
The intruder was a bear
events.same_reason: Phillips and Wikipedia put the hinge at the car on the runway (Wikipedia also at the commander's call); FLI puts it at the pilots' own call to Duluth, before any aircraft moved, and has no car.

entries.actor: an officer's car on the runway
entries.quote: A car raced from command center and successfully signaled the aircraft to stop.
Fortunately, they first established communication with the Duluth center, where they learned that this was not a nuclear attack

entries.label: s6
entries.actor: the base commander's call, then an officer's car
entries.quote: Before the planes were able to take off, the base commander contacted Duluth and learned of the error.
entries.cons_quote: the dangerous possibility of an ADC interceptor accidentally shooting down a Strategic Air Command (SAC) bomber
entries.note: Wikipedia's danger is a different catastrophe: one of our interceptors shooting down one of our bombers.

events.name: Malmstrom: codes in the silo
steps: Minuteman readied in haste; checks skipped
Launch equipment and codes placed in the silo
One operator could launch alone
Missiles put on and off alert as faults are found
events.same_reason: Phillips and FLI both name a single operator at the same moment; Wikipedia names no hinge.

entries.quote: It was thus physically possible for a single operator to launch a fully armed missile at a SIOP target.
entries.cons_quote: launch a fully armed missile at a SIOP target

entries.quote: which would have allowed a single operator to launch a fully armed missile

events.name: Chukotka: a U-2 astray
steps: A U-2 is sent on a new polar route
The aurora spoils navigation; it strays over Chukotka
Soviet MiGs scramble to bring it down
Nuclear-armed F-102As escort it; each pilot can fire
It glides to Alaska
events.same_reason: Three keepers put the hinge in an American pilot's discretion; Chatham House, through Khrushchev's letter, puts it on the Soviet side, in reading the intruder as a bomber.

entries.quote: These could have been used by any one of the F102-A pilots at his own discretion.

entries.actor: the Soviet reading of the U-2 as a bomber
entries.quote: an intruding American plane could be easily taken for a nuclear bomber, which might push us to a fateful step
entries.cons_quote: might push us to a fateful step
entries.note: The words are Khrushchev's, quoted by Chatham House. 'A fateful step' coded as war: my reading.

entries.quote: the pilots had been given orders to shoot at their own discretion

entries.label: s9
entries.quote: Individual pilots were capable of arming and launching their missiles.

events.name: B-59: the torpedo
steps: The notice of practice depth charges is not relayed to the submarines
Practice depth charges hit B-59
The captain orders the nuclear torpedo readied
Launch needs the consent of three officers
Arkhipov refuses and persuades
B-59 surfaces
events.same_reason: All three name Arkhipov at the same moment. Chatham House adds a second officer (Maslennikov, on Orlov's account); FLI puts the luck first in the three-officer rule.

entries.quote: Arkhipov was able to intervene and convince Savitsky he should await instructions from superiors in Moscow
entries.quote2: Ivan Semenovich Maslennikov, had a role in convincing Savitsky

entries.actor: the three-officer rule, and Arkhipov's no
entries.quote: Fortunately, the decision to launch had to be authorized by three officers on board, and one of them, Vasili Arkhipov, said no.

entries.label: s7
entries.quote: Vasily Arkhipov refused permission to launch

events.name: Blackout: two red bomb alarms
steps: Power fails across the northeast
Two bomb alarms show red through circuit errors
The Office of Emergency Planning goes on full alert
The military does not

entries.note: FLI's 'would have' is about what an attack would have looked like, not about what would have followed.

events.name: Thule: a burning bomber
steps: Fire on a B-52 on airborne alert near Thule
The crew bails out with no word to SAC
It crashes; the weapons' high explosive goes off, no nuclear yield
Every line to Thule would have read as an attack
events.same_reason: Phillips and FLI both put the hinge in the weapons' nuclear yield at the crash; Wikipedia names none.

entries.quote: it is believed that a nuclear explosion could have resulted form accidental detonation of the high explosive trigger
entries.cons_quote: all three communication methods would have given an indication consistent with a succsessful nuclear attack

entries.quote: If the nuclear component had exploded
entries.cons_quote: would likely have led SAC to assume that the explosion had been an attack

events.name: Kincheloe: a klaxon under repair
steps: DEFCON 3 during the Middle East crisis
A klaxon repair sets off the whole base alarm
B-52 crews run out and start engines
The duty officer recalls them
events.same_reason: All three name the duty officer at the recall.

entries.quote: if the following accident had not been promptly corrected then the Soviet command might have had a more dangerous interpretation
entries.cons_quote: the Soviet command might have had a more dangerous interpretation

entries.quote: the duty officer realized it was a false alarm, and called them all back, before any further damage was done

entries.label: s13b
entries.quote: nearly scrambled the B-52 bombers at the base before the duty officer declared a false alarm
entries.note: Wikipedia's 'nearly' reaches a scramble, not a war.

events.name: NORAD: an exercise tape
steps: An exercise tape runs on an operational computer
Four command centres see a full Soviet attack
Retaliation is prepared; the airborne command post takes off
Radar and satellites show no missiles
events.same_reason: Only Chatham House names a hinge.

entries.cons_quote: the type of disaster that was threatening at that moment
entries.note: Phillips names a safeguard that was not used, the hot line, but not a point where the outcome turned.

entries.actor: access to the PAVE PAWS radar
entries.quote: Only the ability of NORAD (the North American Aerospace Defense Command) to access the US Air Force's Ballistic Missile Early-Warning System PAVE PAWS radar enabled it to confirm that this alert was false

entries.label: s35
entries.cons_quote: a decision to retaliate would need to be made by the president within three to seven minutes
entries.note: Wikipedia tells the Brzezinski telephone story (250, then 2,200 missiles) under 1979. Chatham House tells it under 3 June 1980.

events.name: NORAD: a faulty chip
steps: A failing chip puts 2s into the missile counters
Retaliation is prepared; bomber crews start engines
Odom's third call reaches Brzezinski a minute before the president would be told
The numbers are judged irrational: a false alarm
It happens again three days later
events.same_reason: Chatham House puts the hinge in the timing of a third telephone call to Brzezinski; FLI puts it in the personnel who read the numbers as illogical.

entries.actor: Odom's third call, a minute early
entries.quote: With only a minute until Brzezinski was to notify the president, Odom telephoned for a third time
entries.note: Coded chance (timing): the entry's weight is on the minute.

entries.actor: the personnel who read the numbers
entries.quote: personnel were able to determine in time that this was a false alarm as the varying missile numbers weren't logical
entries.cons_quote: again B-52 crews and missiles were nearly sent out in retaliation

events.name: Serpukhov-15: Petrov
steps: The satellite system reports five Minuteman launches
Protocol: report upward at once
Petrov reports a false alarm
Cause: sunlight on clouds
events.same_reason: All three name Petrov at his report. Chatham House alone adds that the hinge may not have been one: someone higher up could have concluded the same.

entries.quote: Petrov ultimately reported the incident as a false alarm to his superiors.
entries.quote2: there is the possibility that another decision-maker higher up the chain of command could have come to the same conclusion as Petrov did
entries.note: The only entry of 45 that questions its own hinge.

entries.quote: following procedures would have led him to report an incoming attack

entries.label: s38
entries.quote: Petrov of the Air Defense Forces refused to acknowledge the threat as legitimate

events.name: Able Archer 83
steps: Tension: KAL 007, Operation RYAN, Pershing II
NATO's exercise runs up to a simulated DEFCON 1
Soviet forces raised to alert
Gordievsky tells the West what Moscow fears
The exercise ends; Soviet forces stand down
events.same_reason: Chatham House puts the hinge in Gordievsky's warnings (and also quotes a Soviet officer who denies there was a war scare at all); FLI puts it outside the event, in a second false alarm that did not happen on 11 November.

entries.quote: only Gordievsky's timely warnings to the West kept things from getting out of hand
entries.quote2: believed there was an immediate threat of a nuclear strike from the United States or NATO
entries.note: Chatham House keeps the hinge and its denial side by side: a former CIA historian for it, General Danilevich ('No one ... believed there was an immediate threat') against.

entries.off: a second false alarm on 11 November
entries.quote: what might have happened if an independent incident such as the September 26 1983 false alarm or the 1995 Norwegian Rocket Launch would have randomly occurred on November 11 1983 instead
entries.cons_quote: We may have been at the brink of nuclear war and not even known it.
entries.note: FLI's hinge is built from two other near misses, moved in time.

events.name: The Norwegian rocket
steps: Norway's notice does not reach the radar crews
Radar reads a research rocket as a submarine missile
Yeltsin is handed the briefcase
Satellites show no further launches; the track ends outside Russia
The alarm is cancelled

entries.note: Phillips lists it and says it could hardly have led to retaliation.
entries.note_quote: This particular one could have hardly brought nuclear retaliation.

entries.note: Chatham House: the systems worked; it was mistaken identity.
entries.note_quote: technology and early-warning systems functioned properly but it was a case of 'mistaken identity'

entries.quote: Fortunately Russian satellites monitoring U.S. missile fields did not show any additional launches

observations.text: The same telephone story (Brzezinski woken, first some hundreds of missiles, then 2,200) is told by Wikipedia under 9 November 1979 and by Chatham House under 3 June 1980.
quotes: NORAD computers then placed the number of incoming missiles at 2,200.
it was in fact 2,200 missiles that were headed towards the country

observations.text: The words 'We will die, but we will sink them all' are given by Chatham House to the captain, Valentin Savitsky, and by FLI to 'Valentin Grigorievich, the torpedo officer'.
quotes: Valentin Grigorievich, the torpedo officer, exclaimed
